title: Practical Absolute Entropies Can Be Determined Calorimetrically
lead: With the third law fixing the entropy at 0 K, heat capacities measured on warming a substance, together with the enthalpies of its phase transitions, give its absolute entropy at any temperature. Carbon dioxide, warmed from 0 K to 300 K, is the worked case.
notes: The page names no authors; Figure 21.5.1 is redrawn from the book's curve, read off its image.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise for this section; the one exercise, on the enthalpy of sublimation read from the jump in Figure 21.5.1, was written by AI with an AI solution. Its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. The answer accepts a 3% tolerance, since the entropies are read off a graph.

figures.original_caption: The molar entropy of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ from 0 K to 300 K.

ai.part: built, the curve read off the book's image

exercises.prompt: In Figure 21.5.1 the molar entropy of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ jumps from about 69 J/(mol K) to about 200 J/(mol K) at its sublimation temperature, 194.7 K. Estimate the enthalpy of sublimation of $\mathrm{CO_2}$, in kJ/mol.

answer.solution: The jump is the entropy of sublimation, $\Delta \kSent_{sub} = 200 - 69 = 131$ J/(mol K). By Equation 21.5.2, $\Delta H_{sub} = \kTsub\,\Delta \kSent_{sub} = (194.7\ \text{K})(131\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}) = 2.55\times10^4$ J/mol $= 25.5$ kJ/mol.
